example.answer: At 65 you would have about $1,015,588.82: $220,000 of your own contributions plus $795,588.82 of investment growth.
example.problem: You are 30, plan to retire at 65, have $10,000 saved, contribute $500 a month, and expect a 7% annual return. What will you have at 65?
steps: Years of saving: 65 − 30 = 35 years, which is 420 monthly contributions.
You contributed $10,000 + $500 × 420 = $220,000, so investment growth added $795,588.82.
example.title: Saving from age 30 to 65

faqs.a: A common rule of thumb is 15% of your income, including any employer match. The right number depends on your age, goals, and expected return — try this calculator with different monthly amounts to see what gets you to your target.
faqs.q: How much should I save for retirement each month?

faqs.a: US stocks have averaged roughly 7% per year after inflation over very long periods, but no single decade is guaranteed to match that. Many planners use 5–7% for projections and treat the result as a rough guide.

Yes — a match is free money and it compounds just like your own contributions. If your employer matches 50% of your contributions up to a limit, include that amount in your monthly contribution for a more complete picture.
faqs.q: Should I count my employer's 401(k) match?

faqs.a: You will need larger monthly contributions to catch up, because you have fewer years of compounding. The calculator shows exactly how much more: try the same goal with 20 years instead of 35 and watch the required monthly amount jump.

howItWorks: Retirement savings grow in two ways at once. The money you already have compounds for the full time until you retire, and every monthly contribution you make compounds for the months that remain after you deposit it. The calculator works out the future value of both parts with monthly compounding and adds them together.

Time is the most powerful input here. Because growth compounds, money saved in your 30s works much harder than money saved in your 50s: an extra decade of compounding can more than double the final amount, even with the same monthly contribution. That is why starting early usually beats contributing more later.

This is an estimate for planning purposes, not financial advice. Actual returns vary year to year, and this calculator does not account for inflation, taxes, fees, or employer matching. Use it to compare scenarios, and talk to a qualified financial advisor before making retirement decisions.
intro: See how much your retirement savings could grow by the time you retire. Enter your current age, retirement age, what you have saved, your monthly contribution, and the expected annual return to project your nest egg.

mistakes.text: A 7% annual return is 0.005833 per month, not 0.07. Using 7% monthly would pretend your money grows 125% a year and give a wildly inflated answer.
mistakes.title: Using the annual rate as the monthly rate

mistakes.text: Money you already have keeps growing for the full period. Leaving out the existing $10,000 in the example above would understate the result by over $115,000.
mistakes.title: Forgetting your current savings compound too

mistakes.text: $1 million in 35 years will not buy what $1 million buys today. At 3% inflation it has the buying power of about $355,000 in today's money, so plan with that in mind.
mistakes.title: Ignoring inflation

mistakes.text: A 7% average hides years of losses and gains. Real portfolios bounce around, so treat the projection as one scenario among many, not a promise.
mistakes.title: Assuming the return is guaranteed
